clinician.trajectory_summary: A 39-year-old male presented with severe COVID-19 respiratory illness, confirmed by positive swab and requiring oxygen support. On day 8, he developed acute focal neurological symptoms including reduced GCS, right-sided weakness, hemisensory loss, and diplopia. Brain MRI revealed multiple acute ischemic infarctions in the territories of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery and bilateral posterior cerebral arteries. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) showed multifocal areas of narrowing and occlusions in both posterior cerebral arteries, initially suggestive of CNS vasculitis. However, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was largely unremarkable, with only mildly raised protein and negative viral PCRs, arguing against an inflammatory vasculitis. Systemic inflammatory markers and DSA were not reported. He received a short course of methylprednisolone for possible CNS vasculitis. Despite this, the general specialist consensus favored CNS vasculopathy, likely due to the lack of strong inflammatory evidence and the nature of the vascular changes. The patient also presented with significant cognitive impairments.
